analysis.one_liner: Ends the insurance industry's exemption from antitrust laws against price fixing and monopolies.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it died in the House Judiciary Committee when the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003.
analysis.plain_summary: Since 1945, the McCarran-Ferguson Act has generally let insurance companies escape federal antitrust laws, meaning arrangements to fix prices, divide up territories or customers, or force customers to buy policies they don't want have largely been shielded from prosecution when state insurance law covers them. This bill would have stripped that shield for the worst practices — price fixing, dividing markets, tying one product to another, and monopolizing — while still letting insurers share historical claims data and use actuaries to price policies. It was introduced late in 2002, sent to the House Judiciary Committee, and never received a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers and businesses buying insurance — auto, home, health, liability, and commercial policies — benefit if the bill passes, because insurers could no longer coordinate prices, divide up markets, or tie products together without facing federal antitrust lawsuits the way companies in other industries do. Competitive insurers and businesses in concentrated insurance markets would also benefit from a fairer field.

how_it_helps.text: It would let the Justice Department, the Federal Trade Commission, and private plaintiffs sue insurers over price fixing, market allocation, tying, and monopolization — conduct currently shielded by the McCarran-Ferguson Act when state insurance law covers it.
It would expose arrangements where insurers divide up which customers or regions each serves, which can leave some areas with few insurers and high prices.
It would allow challenges to tying arrangements, such as requiring a customer to buy one type of insurance in order to get another, a practice that limits comparison shopping.

It takes effect a year after enactment and keeps lawful cooperation on historical loss data, loss development factors, and actuarial services, so smaller insurers can continue pooling the data they need to price policies.

analysis.who_pays: Insurance companies bear the cost if the bill passes: they would lose the McCarran-Ferguson shield and could be sued for price fixing, market allocation, tying, and monopolization. To the extent the exemption has propped up higher premiums, the industry's loss is customers' gain.

drawbacks.text: Insurers argue the shared-data activities the exemption protects — pooling historical loss data and setting trend factors — keep pricing accurate and help smaller insurers compete, and the bill had to carve out transition-period allowances for exactly those activities, showing the line between legitimate cooperation and price fixing is not always clean.

Removing the exemption does not itself lower premiums; it only makes insurers potentially liable for price fixing, market allocation, tying, and monopolization under the Sherman and FTC Acts, so enforcement would depend on antitrust agencies and private lawsuits rather than the bill directly capping anything.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is that large insurers could no longer legally fix prices, divide markets, or use dominance in one insurance line to force customers into another, which would put downward pressure on premiums for households and businesses. The cost-side concerns are real but modest: insurers argued that shared industry data and trend factors help small insurers price risk accurately and keep markets stable, and this bill was drafted to address that by continuing to allow historical loss data sharing, actuarial services, and a temporary trend-factor allowance, with a one-year lead time before taking effect. The main design weakness is that antitrust enforcement is slow and costly, so removing the exemption helps mainly where violations are provable rather than wherever prices are simply high.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the House Judiciary Committee, which never acted on it, so it expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Peter DeFazio introduced the Insurance Competitive Pricing Act of 2002 on September 24, 2002.
The House referred it to the Judiciary Committee the same day, and no further action was ever recorded.
The 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003, and the bill died in committee with no hearing, no markup, and no vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Insurance companies kept their McCarran-Ferguson exemption from antitrust liability for price fixing and monopolization, leaving insurance prices to be set under the status quo. Consumers paid whatever the existing system produced.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on the day it was introduced and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — before the Congress expired.

against.name: Insurance industry trade groups
against.what_they_did: The insurance industry has long defended the McCarran-Ferguson antitrust exemption, including against repeal efforts like this bill.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote, so no party split was ever recorded; the sponsor and all four cosponsors were Democrats, and the Republican-led Judiciary Committee took no action.

industries.note: The bill strips away the industry's long-standing exemption from antitrust laws for price fixing, market allocation, tying, and monopolization, exposing insurers to federal antitrust suits the way other industries already are. It protects the data-pooling and actuarial cooperation insurers rely on, so the core loss is the freedom from antitrust liability, which has historically supported higher, coordinated pricing.

industries.industry: Antitrust enforcement (Justice Department and Federal Trade Commission)
industries.note: The bill would give federal antitrust agencies authority over anticompetitive conduct in insurance that state regulation currently shields, expanding their enforcement role.
